title: Presenting a result
objectives: Report a result with its uncertainty, its failure modes and the next step.

screens.title: How far could it move
screens.prose: About three minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. The linear model has a test RMSE of £29.66k on 99 homes. We resample the 99 test rows with replacement, 5,000 times, and recompute the RMSE each time.
screens.question: Where do the middle 95% of the resampled RMSEs lie?

options.text: About £24.9k to £34.2k
£27.7k to £31.7k, two thousand either side of the estimate
options.why: You wrapped a guess around the point estimate. The histogram is wider than that.

options.text: £0 to £85.1k, between zero and the baseline
options.why: That is the range of the problem, not of the estimate.

options.text: Exactly £29.66k, since that is the mean of the resamples
options.why: The resamples scatter around it. The 95% range is a width, not a point.

hints.text: Look for the bars that hold the middle of the histogram.
The ends are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
The bars run from about 25 to 34 before they thin out.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read where the histogram thins out on each side.

byKey.tight: You guessed a width. Read it off the histogram.
byKey.range: You gave the range of prices, not the error.
byKey.mean: You gave a point, not an interval.

explain.text: Cutting 2.5% off each tail leaves £24.87k to £34.22k. That is how far a 99-row test set lets the RMSE move.

screens.title: The half-width
screens.prose: The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 5,000 RMSEs are £24.87k and £34.22k. A report says "about plus or minus" a figure.
screens.question: What is the half-width of the interval, in £k?

hints.text: Subtract the ends first.
The width is 34.22 minus 24.87.
Half of 9.35 is 4.675.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take half of the width.

byKey.width: You gave the full width. Half of it goes either side.

explain.text: The interval is 9.35 wide, so "about £4.7k either side". The ends are not exactly symmetric, which is why we say "about".

screens.title: Against the baseline
screens.prose: On the same 99 rows the training mean scores £85.05k and the model £29.66k. Out-of-sample $R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}_{\text{model}}/\text{SSE}_{\text{baseline}}$.
screens.question: What is the out-of-sample $R^2$?

hints.text: Squared errors share the 99 rows, so the RMSE ratio squared is the SSE ratio.

feedback.correct: 0.8784: the model explains 88% of the squared error the baseline leaves.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square the RMSE ratio, then subtract it from 1.

byKey.cut: You used the plain ratio. $R^2$ compares squared errors.
byKey.left: That is the share of squared error left. $R^2$ is what was removed.

explain.text: The model leaves 12.2% of the baseline’s squared error. The per-row gain averages 6,353.7, with a bootstrap 95% interval of 4,487 to 8,445. That excludes zero.

screens.title: Five sentences
screens.prose: A reader wants the result first and the method last. Put the five sentences in order, and leave out the one that belongs in an appendix.
screens.question: Order the report.

lines.text: The model’s test RMSE is £29.7k on 99 held-out homes.
A bootstrap interval for that error is about £25k to £34k.
The training-mean baseline has an RMSE of £85.1k, so the model cuts the error by about two thirds.
It could fail on mistyped prices, drifting band premiums, or collinear bedrooms and area.
Next I would test on a later period and refit on a rolling window.
I cleaned the file, split it 75/25 and fitted a linear model on eight features.
lines.why: That is the method. Put the result first and the method in an appendix.

hints.text: Result first, then how sure you are.
Then the comparison, the failure modes and the next step.
The sentence about fitting eight features is the method.

feedback.correct: Result, interval, baseline, failure modes, next step.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Lead with the result and end with the next step.

byKey.x: You put the method in the report’s five sentences. A reader wants the result first.
byKey.left-out: You left out a sentence the reader needs.

explain.text: Result, interval, baseline, failure modes, next step. The method goes in an appendix for anyone who wants to rerun it.

screens.title: Just the number
screens.prose: A colleague writes one line: "The model’s RMSE is £29.66k."
screens.question: What is missing?

options.text: How far 99 rows could move it, and the baseline it beats
More decimal places, so that it reads as an exact figure
options.why: Digits are not precision. The interval is the precision.

options.text: The training RMSE too, since it is the smaller number
options.why: Training error flatters. It is not a check.

options.text: Nothing: a single number is already a full result
options.why: A number on 99 rows could be £5k either way.

hints.text: Ask how sure the number is.
A test set of 99 rows is small.
The reader needs the interval and what the number is compared with.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what a reader needs to trust the number.

byKey.digits: You added decimals. They imply a precision the data lack.
byKey.train: You added training error, which flatters.

explain.text: A point estimate from 99 rows can move by about £4.7k either way. Report the interval and the baseline beside it.

screens.title: More test rows
screens.prose: On 99 test rows the interval is £9.35k wide. Suppose the test set had 396 rows, four times as many, with the same spread of errors.
screens.question: Roughly how wide would the interval be, in £k?

hints.text: Interval width shrinks with the square root of the rows.
Four times the rows is twice as precise.
Half of 9.35 is about 4.7.

feedback.correct: About £4.7k: four times the rows halves the width.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Width falls with the root of the number of rows.

byKey.quarter: You quartered it. Width falls with the root of the rows, so it halves.

explain.text: Width goes as $1/\sqrt{n}$, so four times the rows halves it. An interval on 99 rows is wide because 99 is small.

screens.title: Say it aloud
screens.prose: The report is the estimate, its interval and the baseline in one sentence: $\hat{\theta}$, then $[\theta_{2.5}, \theta_{97.5}]$, then $\theta_{\text{base}}$. Then the failure modes and the next step.
screens.question: Which result sentence would you say?

options.text: RMSE £29.7k, about £25k to £34k, against a baseline of £85.1k.
The model is 88% accurate, which is a strong result overall.
options.why: Accuracy is a classification score. This is a price, with an error in pounds.

options.text: I think the model works well, and I would trust it a lot.
options.why: You gave no number to check.

options.text: The RMSE is £29.66k, plus or minus £0.01k on the 99 homes.
options.why: You gave a precision the 99 rows cannot give.

hints.text: Look for three numbers in one sentence.
The estimate, the interval and the baseline.
Only one option has all three.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the sentence with three numbers.

byKey.acc: You used accuracy for a price. The score is an error in pounds.
byKey.vague: You gave an opinion, not a number.
byKey.tight: You claimed a precision the data lack.

explain.text: One sentence with the estimate, the interval and the baseline. Failure modes and the next step follow.

screens.title: Where the interval comes from
screens.prose: We want the spread of the test RMSE without collecting new homes. We reuse the 99 test rows we have.
screens.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Draw 99 rows from the test set with replacement, so some repeat and some are missing.
Compute the RMSE of the model on that resample.
Repeat 5,000 times to get 5,000 RMSEs, which show how the figure moves.
Sort them and read the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
Drop the 2.5% of rows with the largest errors and recompute.
lines.why: Trimming the worst rows makes the error look smaller. It does not measure how much it could move.

hints.text: Resample, score, repeat, then read the percentiles.
Each resample is a possible test set of the same size.
The middle 95% of 5,000 scores is the interval.

feedback.correct: The percentile bootstrap: resample, score, repeat, read the ends.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Draw, score, repeat, sort.

byKey.x: You trimmed the worst rows. That hides the spread instead of measuring it.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the method needs.

explain.text: Each resample is a plausible test set. Their 5,000 scores show how far the RMSE could move, and the percentiles give the 95% interval.

screens.title: Report the spread model
screens.prose: On 200 test days the spread AR(1) scores 1.1533 against 1.2071 for yesterday’s value, a 4.46% gain. The per-day gain in squared error has $t = 1.87$ and a bootstrap 95% interval of about −0.002 to 0.111.
screens.question: Which sentence is supportable?

options.text: About 4.5% better, but the interval touches zero
It is clearly better, since 4.46% is a gain on yesterday
options.why: You read the point estimate and ignored the interval.

options.text: It is worse, since the interval includes a negative value
options.why: The interval touches zero. That makes it unproven, not worse.

options.text: It is 4.46% better, plus or minus 0.01% at most
options.why: You claimed a precision the 200 days cannot give.

hints.text: Check whether zero is inside the interval.
It runs from just below zero to 0.111.
A gain that may be zero is unproven.

feedback.correct: Unproven: the estimate is positive, the interval touches zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Say what the interval allows.

byKey.exact: You claimed a precision the data lack.

explain.text: The five sentences work on any model. Here the interval is the story: a gain of 4.5% that may be nothing.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: "What would make you distrust this result?"
screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: The test rows come from a different period than the period of use
A new postcode band appears that the model never saw
The model was tuned many times on the same test rows
The RMSE is quoted to two decimal places in the report
options.why: Decimals are style. They do not change how the model behaves.

options.text: The model is linear, not a forest or a neural network
options.why: A linear model that beats the baseline on unseen rows is fine.

hints.text: Think of what could change between testing and use.
A new period, a new category, a reused test set.
Three of the five options break the link between the test and the future.

feedback.correct: A different period, a new band and repeated tuning.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick what breaks the link between test and use.

byKey.decimals: Decimals are style, not a risk.
byKey.linear: Linear is fine if it beats the baseline on unseen rows.

explain.text: A new period, an unseen category and a test set used many times all weaken the result. Each one is a reason to retest.

ideas: Report in five sentences: result, interval, baseline, failure modes, next step.
A bootstrap resamples the test rows and reads percentiles. The interval is wide when the test set is small.
An interval that touches zero means a gain is unproven, not absent.
